incidents.title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
incidents.summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become the target of an artificial intelligence scam targeting vulnerable immigrants. Criminals have created hundreds of fake videos and social media profiles using AI-generated images of Leal to deceive people seeking immigration help. In these fraudulent videos, a digital version of Leal offers services like US residency assistance in exchange for cash payments of around $2,200. The scams typically direct victims to contact numbers through WhatsApp, where fraudsters send fake contracts and collect money through payment apps like Venmo and Zelle.

Leal discovered the scheme when potential clients began calling his office about services he never offered. Although suspicious activity began last October, the situation has dramatically worsened over the past three months. His firm hired an anti-piracy company that has successfully removed nearly 6,500 fake profiles across multiple platforms, including 3,500 on TikTok, 2,400 on Facebook, and 544 on Instagram. Leal plans to contact local and federal authorities this week to investigate the scams. He warns immigrants to verify anyone offering legal services online and avoid those requesting immediate payment through digital payment apps.

incidents.title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception
incidents.summary:
A fake online article featuring Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock and ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler has highlighted a growing type of scam. The fabricated article described an increasingly heated interview between the two, with Bullock supposedly objecting to questions about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The confrontation never actually occurred. Australian Securities and Investments Commission research shows that AI-generated investment scams using deepfake images and videos of celebrities and politicians are becoming more common and convincing. Last year, regulators took down 19,400 scams, up 182 percent, with phishing scams rising 279 percent and fake investment platforms increasing 151 percent.

Scammers now build elaborate webs of deception using fake news articles, reviews, websites, and advertisements to lure victims. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is the most commonly impersonated figure, followed by other politicians and financial experts including Kohler, who has previously experienced similar scams. ASIC chair Sarah Court advises potential investors to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through the regulator's public registers and avoid investing if companies cannot provide legitimate credentials. Alan Kohler argues that penalties should extend to platforms hosting this content and companies creating the AI models used in scams.

incidents.title: Sleep Staging Is Not Guesswork
incidents.summary:
A class-action lawsuit filed by Clarkson Law Firm has accused Oura, a smart ring company valued at eleven billion dollars, of false advertising regarding its sleep tracking capabilities. The suit alleges that Oura's rings, which cost three hundred dollars and up, cannot accurately detect sleep stages as claimed in marketing materials. The lawsuit contends that the devices rely on artificial intelligence guesses no better than coin flips, rather than genuine physiological measurements, since the rings lack the complex electrode technology found in clinical sleep labs.

Oura has responded by defending its science and accuracy claims, stating that its rings estimate sleep stages using multiple physiological signals and have been validated against the gold standard polysomnography testing in peer-reviewed studies. The company emphasizes that while its products are not medical devices or substitutes for clinical sleep studies, they provide useful health estimates. It remains unclear whether current customers can join the suit or what compensation may result, though this represents the second lawsuit against Oura, following a previous class-action alleging unauthorized collection of customer data.

incidents.title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Security researchers at Gambit Security discovered that the Aurora ransomware group has been actively targeting ESXi virtual machine environments since April 2026. The group developed a Linux variant of their ransomware that encrypts virtual machine files while keeping the hypervisor operational so victims can read ransom demands. Aurora operators also used Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation attacks against ten organizations between April and May 2026. The group maintains a data leak site and operates across multiple countries.

In a separate investigation, researchers identified a second cluster of Aurora activity with medium confidence, targeting eight organizations across Israel, Germany, Austria, Spain, the United States, and Argentina. This second group used different tactics including SQL Server exploitation, privilege escalation, and data exfiltration to self-hosted storage. Gambit Security published technical indicators of compromise, including command and control server addresses, proxy IP addresses, and file hashes to help organizations identify and defend against these threats.

incidents.title: A Pizza Hut franchisee is suing over a forced AI system it says wrecked deliveries
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Chaac Pizza Northeast, a major Pizza Hut franchisee operating about 111 restaurants across the Northeast, filed a lawsuit in May alleging that Pizza Hut's mandatory adoption of Dragontail, an AI-powered delivery management system, caused over $100 million in damages. The franchisee claims the system allowed DoorDash drivers to see real-time kitchen workflows and order timing, causing them to wait up to 15 minutes to batch multiple orders together instead of delivering immediately, resulting in cold pizzas and poor customer satisfaction. In New York City, year-over-year sales dropped from positive 10.19% growth to negative 9.78% following the rollout in 2024.

Chaac alleges Pizza Hut breached its franchise agreement by forcing the continued use of Dragontail without adequate training or support, despite worsening delivery metrics and plummeting sales. Before the system's implementation, the franchisee maintained over 90% on-time deliveries and consistently outperformed other Pizza Hut operators. Pizza Hut declined to comment beyond saying it would respond through appropriate legal channels. The lawsuit comes as Pizza Hut's parent company, Yum! Brands, faces broader struggles with the brand and plans to close 250 US locations.

incidents.title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Scammers have been impersonating Terry Gross and other "Fresh Air" staff members to defraud authors, entertainers, and public figures. The fraudulent emails appear highly personalized with references to the targets' work and proposed interview topics, but eventually ask recipients to pay fees for production costs. Historian Jennifer Black from Misericordia University received such an email and initially believed it was legitimate until she was asked to pay $250, at which point she contacted WHYY security. WHYY, NPR, and law enforcement are investigating the scheme, which has also targeted comedians like Bruce Vilanch and extended to impersonations of other celebrities including Katie Couric and Amy Poehler.

According to cybersecurity expert Aunshul Rege, artificial intelligence has made these social engineering scams more convincing and personalized than traditional fraud attempts. Red flags include emails from unofficial addresses like "terrygrossfreshair@gmail.com" and requests for payment or login credentials. WHYY clarified that it never charges guests for interviews and stated that any communication requesting fees should be treated as illegitimate. Experts recommend verifying suspicious requests through official organization contacts rather than responding to the fraudulent messages.

incidents.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda
incidents.summary:
# Summary

An Israeli-funded fake think tank called the Hanover Institute published over 560,000 words in nine days across 124 reports designed to influence artificial intelligence chatbots. The website, which doesn't exist as a legal entity and has no named staff, presents pro-Israel arguments on controversial topics including allegations of genocide and war crimes in Gaza. The organization was registered with the U.S. Justice Department as a foreign agent working for the Israeli government through intermediaries, including European advertising group Havas Media. The reports use academic formatting and citations to appear credible while strategically framing information to minimize criticism of Israel.

The campaign is part of a larger Israeli government effort costing tens of millions of dollars to manipulate AI training data and chatbot responses. Israeli officials have privately expressed frustration about the campaign's failure to improve public opinion, which has significantly turned against Israel among Americans. Research shows the operation succeeded in altering some chatbot outputs, but failed to move polling numbers, indicating the underlying political issues rather than messaging are driving American attitudes about Israel.

incidents.title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.
incidents.summary:
Major record labels, including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Capitol Records, and Atlantic Records, have filed separate lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular AI music generators. The labels accuse both companies of scraping massive amounts of copyrighted music without permission and directly reproducing sections of famous songs in their AI-generated outputs. The lawsuits claim the companies deliberately concealed what music they used for training their models, though both previously claimed their use of copyrighted material constituted fair use.

To support their case, the record labels created AI-generated songs using specific prompts and demonstrated they could reproduce versions of famous works by artists including The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Bruce Springsteen, Michael Jackson, and Mariah Carey. They submitted thousands of copyrighted works they claim were scraped for training data, along with a thumb drive of AI-generated examples showing similarities to originals. The lawsuits target both companies and unnamed individuals who allegedly helped scrape the music, setting up a major legal battle over how generative AI services handle copyrighted material.

UMG's CEO stated the company remains committed to supporting artists while embracing new technologies. Udio, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees and backed by investors including musician will.i.am, has attracted millions of users since launching. The financial terms of the settlement were not disclosed. Additionally, UMG announced a separate partnership with London-based Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers.

incidents.title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings
incidents.summary:
# Summary

State Farm's defense lawyers apologized for submitting court filings containing artificial intelligence-generated fabricated legal cases, fake quotes, and nonexistent legal holdings in a Los Angeles lawsuit. The case involves Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, who sued State Farm after a 2020 fire destroyed her Carson home. She claimed the insurance company delayed approving repairs, and when a storm caused additional water damage during reconstruction, the work was never completed. Meni-Siliga stated that she and her husband exhausted their savings, retirement accounts, and eventually lost their home to foreclosure.

Lawyer Jacquelene Robinson admitted using an AI tool called Irys to prepare motions, mistakenly believing it was connected to her firm's legal research subscription and would verify citations. She confirmed that seven case citations across eight filings did not exist, along with incorrect case titles and fabricated quotes. Kenneth Katel, the lead trial counsel, accepted responsibility for the filings. The case is scheduled to go to trial in October. This incident reflects a growing trend, as 41 percent of law firms now use generative AI, though a database documents nearly 1,900 documented legal hallucination cases worldwide.

stories.Headline: China promotes coordinated development of data industry, artificial intelligence-- Beijing Review
stories.Summary:
# Summary

China's data industry reached 6.78 trillion yuan in 2025, and the country is now focusing on coordinating development between its data sector and artificial intelligence capabilities. The 2026 China International Big Data Industry Expo, held in Guiyang from August 28-30, attracted 372 companies and over 16,000 guests to showcase innovations in computing power, large models, and data circulation. Government officials emphasized that high-quality datasets are essential for advancing AI capabilities and that data technology is transforming traditional industries like power generation and renewable energy forecasting.

Beyond upgrading existing industries, data and AI are creating new business opportunities and employment categories. Companies are hiring data collectors to train robots through embodied intelligence projects, while micro-enterprises and one-person startups are emerging as signs of entrepreneurial growth. International participants from Zimbabwe, Chile, Pakistan, and other nations attended to explore cooperation opportunities, with officials highlighting the potential for shared benefits and technological exchange between countries through collaborative data and AI development.

stories.Headline: Who Writes AI's Rules When Someone Else Owns the Machines?
stories.Summary:
# Summary

South Africa withdrew its Draft National AI Policy in April 2026 after discovering that at least six of its 67 academic references were fabricated, highlighting a broader challenge facing the Global South. The incident underscores a critical debate about who controls artificial intelligence governance and infrastructure. Currently, the United States and China host roughly 86% of global data centre capacity, giving them power to set rules and prices for AI systems worldwide. This concentration of computing power represents what critics call "tech colonialism," where developing nations provide data and demand but lack ownership and control over the technology itself.

BRICS countries and other Global South nations are attempting to shift AI governance away from Western-led standards by emphasizing digital sovereignty and development rights. They are seeking to anchor AI governance within the United Nations rather than OECD-led bodies and have established organizations like the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation. However, meaningful sovereignty requires owning physical infrastructure, not just adopting policies. The article notes that until developing nations build regional computing capacity and chip manufacturing capabilities, they remain dependent on foreign platforms controlled by American hyperscalers or Chinese firms. True sovereignty means choosing dependencies rather than having them imposed.

Taiwan's government plans to invest over 40 billion Taiwan dollars, approximately 1.26 billion US dollars, to develop 10 major artificial intelligence projects next year. President William Lai has set an ambitious goal to train at least 500,000 AI professionals by 2040. The administration launched the AI Talent Ark Project this year to nurture talent through fundamental education, professional development, and data-driven approaches, aiming to build a large AI talent pool and strengthen Taiwan's competitiveness in technology sectors.

The government is also prioritizing technological sovereignty and national resilience. The Minister of Digital Affairs announced plans to accumulate at least 10,000 graphics processing units through private investment in AI computing centers within a year. Taiwan is focusing on developing sovereign AI systems that understand Taiwanese perspectives and languages, along with low-Earth-orbit satellite communications to ensure independent communication capabilities. Officials emphasized that technological sovereignty means focusing on critical technologies rather than developing every technology domestically.

stories.Headline: CSA's Top Cloud Threats: Identity, AI -- Campus Technology
stories.Summary:
The Cloud Security Alliance surveyed 507 security professionals to identify the top threats to cloud computing in 2026. Identity and access management issues rose to the number one concern, moving up from second place in 2024, while misconfiguration dropped to fifth. Two artificial intelligence-related threats appeared in the rankings for the first time, including AI-enhanced attacks and AI system compromise. The top eleven threats also include insecure third-party resources, insecure APIs, advanced persistent threats, and inadequate cloud security strategy and governance.

The survey results reveal a significant shift in the cloud threat landscape, with organizations now prioritizing identity protection, artificial intelligence risks, and software supply chains over infrastructure-focused concerns. Security scores ranged closely from 7.95 for identity and access management to 7.45 for system vulnerabilities. The report aims to help organizations make informed risk-management decisions about cloud adoption by providing expert analysis of technical and business impacts, real-world examples, and corresponding security controls across cloud and AI environments.

stories.Headline: EU places ChatGPT, Reddit, Roblox under strictest platform rules
stories.Summary:
The European Union has classified ChatGPT as a Very Large Online Search Engine and designated Reddit and Roblox as Very Large Online Platforms under its Digital Services Act. These three American companies will now face direct supervision from the European Commission and must comply with stricter requirements designed to address risks related to children, election integrity, and public security. The rules apply to services with over 45 million users in the EU, bringing the total number of regulated platforms to 28.

Companies failing to meet the new requirements within four months face fines up to 6 percent of their annual global revenue. Reddit reported 57.2 million EU users in July, while Roblox has 46.6 million. OpenAI stated it would prepare to meet ChatGPT's additional obligations, and Roblox welcomed the designation, emphasizing safety's importance. This designation adds another regulatory layer for ChatGPT, which already complies with the EU's Artificial Intelligence Act.

# Summary

The article argues that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, not Nvidia or AMD, will be the ultimate winner in the artificial intelligence hardware race. While many investors focus on chip designers like Nvidia and AMD, the author contends that Taiwan Semiconductor holds the real advantage because it manufactures chips for these companies and controls approximately 72 percent of the global foundry market. Since Nvidia and AMD do not build their own chips, they must rely on Taiwan Semiconductor's manufacturing capacity.

Taiwan Semiconductor benefits from a neutral position in the competition between chip designers, meaning it will profit regardless of which company's hardware becomes dominant. The company's CEO expects elevated demand for chips to continue through at least 2029 or 2030, providing several more years of strong growth. Additionally, Taiwan Semiconductor plans to launch new chip technology that will allow for price increases, positioning it as one of the safest investments in the artificial intelligence sector.
